public_rationale: The claim says that for essentially everything LLMs talk about, nearly any generalization can be easily broken under distribution shift. The period assessed runs from January 2022 to the post date, 12 March 2023. Shi et al. (first posted 31 January 2023) found that LLM accuracy on grade-school math 'dramatically decreased' when irrelevant information was added. The same study reported ways to reduce this drop. Razeghi et al. (first posted 15 February 2022) found that accuracy on numerical tasks depended on how often terms appeared in pretraining. Lewkowycz et al. (29 June 2022) reported that Minerva 540B scored over 80% on 10-digit addition and over 20% on 18-digit addition. That is a partial counterexample on one arithmetic task. All three studies concern math or numerical tasks. None tests the claim's cross-domain scope, and 'easily broken' has no set threshold. The cited evidence neither confirms nor refutes the claim.
limitations: All the evidence comes from math and numerical tasks, not the range of domains the claim covers.
The contract notes that 'easily broken' does not say how large an input change counts.
The copy of e1 that was observed is a version revised in June 2023, after the post. The finding is attributed to the first version from January 2023.
The Minerva figure covers addition only and does not test other kinds of distribution shift.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: For essentially everything an LLM talks about, there is a degree of generalization to similar examples, but distribution shift is hard and nearly any generalization can be easily broken.
conditions: essentially everything an LLM talks about

statement.excerpt: The same goes for essentially everything an LLMs talks about; there is a degree of generalization to similar examples, but distribution shift is hard (the crux of my own work going back to 1998), and nearly any generalization can be easily broken.

from_speaker: essentially everything an LLM talks about
a degree of generalization to similar examples
nearly any generalization can be easily broken
our_interpretation: Plain reading: across nearly all domains, LLMs of the time generalize to inputs similar to their training data, but small or moderate changes to inputs (distribution shift) easily break that generalization.
Target period: LLMs as studied from 2022-01 to the post date (2023-03-12). This is my choice, because the claim describes a present state without naming a period.
criteria.support_condition: Robustness and distribution-shift studies of contemporary LLMs show, across many domains, that performance collapses under small or modest input changes, with few robust exceptions.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Studies of contemporary LLMs show robust generalization under distribution shift in a broad range of domains, so 'nearly any' generalization does not break easily.

evidence.explanation: Shows a generalization (grade-school math) broken by a small, irrelevant change to the input. It supports brittleness in one domain, and the authors also report ways to reduce it.

evidence.excerpt: our results raise the question of how much models actually generalize beyond pretraining data
evidence.explanation: Consistent with generalization limited to cases like the training data, but limited to numerical tasks in GPT-style models trained on the Pile.

evidence.explanation: Minerva held over 80% accuracy on 10-digit addition, far from typical training examples. That is generalization that did not break easily, though it fell off at 18 digits.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: A robustness evaluation of LLMs from 2022 to early 2023, covering many domains, that measured how often their generalizations failed under small input changes.
